title: Locks, atomics and deadlocks
subtitle: Two threads that touch the same data can quietly break it. Locks and atomics stop that, and lock order stops the deadlocks that locks can cause.

c.v: This is a made-up example, but the bug in it is real. A team runs a small API that counts video views. Each request starts a

In production, traffic is high and the server has many CPU cores. The dashboard shows fewer views than the access logs. The gap is small, so nobody notices for weeks. There is no error and no
The bug is easy to reproduce. The OSTEP textbook runs two threads that each add 1 to a shared counter 10 million times. The answer should be 20,000,000.
Sometimes the book gets the right answer. But one run gave 19,345,221, and the next gave 19,221,041.
Wrong totals that change from run to run are the mark of a

Shared data that changes needs one of three things: a lock, so only one thread is inside at a time; an atomic operation, so the change cannot be split; or no sharing at all.

With CAS you read the value, compute the new one, and try to swap. If another thread changed it first, the swap fails and you try again. OSTEP shows how locks themselves are built from instructions like this.

Java's docs say the gain is fully seen only on a multi-processor, and only when data is read often and changed rarely. If reads are very short, the extra cost of the lock can eat the gain.

OSTEP lists four conditions, which it credits to a 1971 paper by Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani. All four must hold for a deadlock:
A thread has a resource, such as a lock, to itself.
A thread holds some locks while it waits for more.
Nobody can take a lock away from its holder.
There is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a lock the next one holds.
Break any one condition and deadlock cannot happen.

The same ideas in a database
A database has the same problems, one level up. Two requests that read a row, add 1 in app code, and write it back can lose an update. The
Row locks can deadlock too. The Postgres docs show two
that update the same two accounts in opposite order. Postgres detects the deadlock and aborts one of them. Which one is hard to predict.
The fix is the same as in memory. Postgres says the best defence is to take locks on many objects in a consistent order.

c.v: When you see shared state that changes, ask "who else writes this?" first. This one question finds many race bugs.
Prefer no sharing, then atomics for one value, then a mutex. Use a read-write lock only after a profile shows it helps.
Write the lock order down in a comment or in the
, and keep it the same in every code path.
Never call the network or wait on I/O while you hold a lock.
Run your tests with a race detector where the language has one.
In SQL, update rows in a fixed order, for example by ID, and retry on deadlock errors.
For a distributed lock, ask whether it is for efficiency or for correctness. For correctness, use fencing tokens, or better, a database constraint.
When a bug "only happens under load" and the numbers are a little off, suspect a race condition.

A "thread-safe" claim is tested with many threads and many runs, not one run.
No lock is held across a network call or a callback.

q.v: once. The counter starts at 7. With no lock, what can the result be?

why.v: Both threads can load 7 before either stores. Then both store 8, and one add is lost.

q.v: Which change removes the circular wait that causes most deadlocks?

options.v: Make every thread take locks in the same global order.

why.v: If everyone takes lock 1 before lock 2, no thread can hold 2 while waiting for 1, so no cycle can form.

options.v: It writes a new value only if the variable still holds the value you expected, and tells you if it worked.
It swaps two variables in memory.
It locks the variable until you unlock it.

why.v: Go's docs describe it as one atomic step. If the value equals old, set it to new and return true. Otherwise return false.

q.v: Postgres finds that two transactions wait for each other's row locks. What happens?

options.v: Postgres aborts one of them, so the other can finish. The app should retry.

why.v: Postgres detects deadlocks and aborts one transaction. Which one is hard to predict.

q.v: A lease-based distributed lock expires while the holder is stuck in a long GC pause. What stops the old holder's late write?

options.v: A fencing token that the storage checks on every write.

why.v: Kleppmann shows that the storage must reject writes that carry an older token than one it has already seen.
